\subsection{Avalanche Ionization}
\label{sec:avalanche}

The energy shift is given by $\Delta E = \hbar\omega_0 \pm \hbar\omega_q$, where $\hbar\omega_q$ is the phonon energy and $\hbar\omega_0$ is the photon energy. Since the phonon energy is very small compared to the photon energy, we can assume $\Delta E \approx \hbar\omega_0$. Electrons can absorb several photons in sequence, increasing their velocity and their energy. Beyond a certain threshold, the energy of the free carriers exceeds the gap energy, and they can then collide with electrons of the valence band, causing impact ionization. This leaves two electrons in the conduction band, which increases the absorption efficiency and triggers further impact ionization events. This cascading effect is known as avalanche ionization. It combines free carrier absorption with impact ionization, sketched in Figure~\ref{fig:avalanche_cascade}.

        \draw[thick] (0,\cond) node[left=10pt] {CB} -- (7.8,\cond);
        \draw[thick, dashed] (0,\crit) node[left=10pt] {Critical energy ($E_{\text{crit}}$)} -- (7.8,\crit);

        \draw[<->, >=Stealth] (-1.2, \val+0.1) -- (-1.2, \cond-0.1) node[midway, left, align=center] {Ionization\\potential};
        \draw[<->, >=Stealth] (-1.2, \cond) -- (-1.2, \crit-0.3) node[midway, left, align=center] {Kinetic energy for\\impact ionization};

        \def\xone{1}
        \node[elec] (e1_v) at (\xone, \val) {};
        \node[elec] (e1_c) at (\xone, \cond) {};

        \def\xtwo{3}
        \node[elec] (e1_crit) at (\xtwo, \crit) {};

        \def\xthree{3.5}
        \node[elec] (e1_drop) at (\xthree, \cond) {};
        \node[elec] (e2_v) at (\xthree+0.2, \val) {};
        \node[elec] (e2_rise) at (\xthree+0.2, \cond) {};
        \draw[arrow] (e1_crit) -- (e1_drop);

        \draw[arrow] (e1_crit2) -- (e1_drop2);
        \draw[arrow] (e2_crit2) -- (e2_drop2);

        \node[above, align=center] at (\xsix+0.2, \crit+0.2) {Avalanche chain reaction};

        \draw[thick] (6, 0.5) rectangle (7.8, 1.5);

    }
    \caption{Avalanche chain reaction. A seed electron is promoted to the conduction band by photoionization, heated above the critical energy $E_{\text{crit}}$ by successive inverse Bremsstrahlung absorption, and knocks a second valence electron into the conduction band by impact ionization. Both electrons repeat the cycle, doubling the population at each generation.}
    \label{fig:avalanche_cascade}
\end{figure}

This process can repeat itself as long as the electric field is present and intense enough.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{fig10_avalanche_vs_time.png}
    \caption{On-axis electron density at fixed $z=57\ \mu$m with and without the avalanche term $\sigma_\omega I N/U_i$ of Eq.~\eqref{eq:master_propagation}, reproducing Fig.~10 of~\cite{PhysRevB.71.125435} at $1.1\ \mu$J, $800\ \text{nm}$. Photoionization alone (dashed) already produces a plateau once the pulse has passed, but avalanche multiplication (solid) drives the final density roughly a factor of six higher, showing that impact ionization contributes substantially to the total carrier yield once seeded by the multiphoton channel, even for the $\sim100\ \text{fs}$ pulse duration used here.}
    \label{fig:fig10_avalanche}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \repfig[0.8\linewidth]{rep_avalanche_takeover.png}
    \caption{Seeding and takeover, on axis at the most intense plane of the $5\ \mu$J, $1030\ \text{nm}$ run. Top: the free electron density $\rho_e$ (black, log scale) against the local intensity (orange, linear). Bottom: the total creation rate $\mathrm{d}\rho_e/\mathrm{d}t$ split into the avalanche term $\beta I \rho_e (1-\rho_e/\rho_{max})$ of Eq.~\eqref{eq:master_propagation} and the remainder, which is the photoionization contribution. The two curves cross well before the pulse peak: photoionization alone sets the seed density, after which impact ionization supplies almost all of the growth. This is the quantitative form of the statement made above that the cascade must first be started by another mechanism, since $\beta I \rho_e$ vanishes when $\rho_e$ does.}
    \label{fig:rep_avalanche_takeover}
\end{figure}

\authornote{The avalanche coefficient plotted here is $\beta=\sigma_\omega/U_i$ evaluated with the collision time \texttt{tau\_c} used by the solver, $1.7\ \text{fs}$ ($\omega_0\tau_c\approx3$). Couairon et al.~\cite{PhysRevB.71.125435} instead calibrate $\tau_c=10\ \text{fs}$ ($\omega_0\tau_c\approx24$) against transmission measurements. Because $\sigma_\omega\propto\tau_c/(1+\omega_0^2\tau_c^2)$ is non-monotonic, the shorter time gives the \emph{larger} cross section, and the resulting $\beta$ differs by about a factor five between the two conventions. The final density that follows differs by several orders of magnitude, so this figure should be read as showing the mechanism, not as a calibrated prediction of $\rho_e$, until the choice of $\tau_c$ is settled.}
